es: Sustituir afirmaciones absolutas por generalizaciones matizadas con tend to, by and large, as a rule e it is not unusual for.

teaching.en: An absolute statement such as “All teenagers are lazy” collapses as soon as you meet one exception, so careful speakers avoid it.
teaching.es: Una afirmación absoluta como «Todos los adolescentes son perezosos» se derrumba en cuanto conoces una excepción, así que los hablantes cuidadosos la evitan.
teaching.explanationEs: Todos, siempre y nunca son absolutos: casi nunca son justos.

teaching.en: Typical travellers return with a sweeping generalisation about a whole nation and forget everyone they did not meet.
teaching.es: Los viajeros típicos vuelven con una generalización demasiado amplia sobre toda una nación y olvidan a todos los que no conocieron.
teaching.explanationEs: Una generalización amplia habla de la prisa del viajero, no de la gente.

teaching.en: People in my town tend to be punctual and, with few exceptions, they apologise when they are late.
teaching.es: En mi ciudad la gente suele ser puntual y, con pocas excepciones, se disculpa cuando llega tarde.
teaching.explanationEs: Tend to + verbo base expresa tendencia; with few exceptions la reconoce.
segments: People in my town tend to be punctual and,
with few exceptions, they apologise when they are late.
teaching.audioText: People in my town tend to be punctual and, with few exceptions, they apologise when they are late.

teaching.en: By and large, my neighbours are reserved at first but, more often than not, they turn out to be warm and generous.
teaching.es: En general, mis vecinos son reservados al principio pero, la mayoría de las veces, resultan ser cálidos y generosos.
teaching.explanationEs: By and large abre la frase; more often than not matiza con frecuencia, no con certeza.

teaching.explanationEs: It is not unusual for + sujeto + to + verbo: «no es raro que».

teaching.en: To qualify a claim without weakening it, replace absolute words such as all and never with tend to, most or usually.
teaching.es: Para matizar una afirmación sin debilitarla, sustituye palabras absolutas como all y never por tend to, most o usually.
teaching.explanationEs: Matizar no es dudar: es ajustar lo que dices a lo que puedes sostener.

prompt.es: ¿Qué versión corrige mejor la frase absoluta de la estudiante?

choices.text: Nobody in that city is ever on time, and all of them are rude.
Some people there are sometimes late, but they always apologise.
People there tend to be late, and many do not apologise.

feedback.es: Tend to y many sustituyen a everybody, always y nobody: la versión conserva la observación sin convertirla en ley.

hint.es: Busca la versión sin todos, siempre ni nadie.

origin.text: A student wrote in her travel blog: “Everybody in that city is always late, and nobody ever apologises.” Her teacher underlined the absolute words and asked for a more careful version.

prompt.es: Completa: «Por norma general, las tiendas cierran pronto los domingos.»

feedback.es: As a rule es la fórmula fija para «por norma general» y admite excepciones, como las tiendas para turistas.

origin.text: Shops here are not all the same, but as a ___, they close early on Sundays, and a few stay open for tourists.

prompt.es: Ordena: «No es raro que la gente coma tarde.»

answer.text: It is not unusual for people to eat late

feedback.es: It is not unusual for + sujeto + to + verbo base: «no es raro que» con sujeto propio.

hint.es: Empieza con it is not unusual for.

prompt.es: Escucha: ¿qué defecto tiene la afirmación del hermano?

choices.text: It describes the north with too many exceptions.
It depends on one conversation with a taxi driver.
It generalises from a tiny sample to everybody.
It ignores that waiters are often reserved.

feedback.es: Cuatro personas no representan a todo un lugar: el error está en pasar de una muestra mínima a un «all» absoluto.

origin.audio: After a week in the north, my brother came back saying that all the locals were cold. I asked him how many he had actually spoken to. Four, he admitted: a taxi driver, two waiters and a man in a queue. I told him that four people do not make a nation, and that he could safely say only that the people he met had been rather reserved.

prompt.es: Lee el párrafo: ¿qué postura mantiene quien escribe?

choices.text: Every statement about teenagers is unfair and should be avoided.
Teenagers sleep late because they are lazy and tired.
The habit of sleeping late is the same in every family.
A general pattern is acceptable if it admits exceptions.

feedback.es: Acepta el patrón («tend to»), pero rechaza que valga para todos: la versión segura dice «many» y reconoce la variación.

origin.text: Teachers often say that teenagers tend to sleep late, and this is mostly true. But it is not true of all teenagers, and I know several who are awake at six. The safest statement is that many teenagers prefer later hours, and that the habit varies from one family to another.

prompt.es: Ordena: «Con pocas excepciones, aquí la gente suele ser puntual.»

answer.text: With few exceptions, people here tend to be punctual
accepted: With few exceptions, people here tend to be punctual
People here tend to be punctual, with few exceptions

feedback.es: With few exceptions puede abrir o cerrar la frase; tend to va seguido de un verbo base (be).

prompt.es: Escucha: ¿cuál es la postura de la investigadora sobre las generalizaciones?

choices.text: It is fair to notice a pattern, but wrong to present it as a rule with no exceptions.
Travellers should avoid forming any impression of a country from one visit.
Tiredness explains why some people are unfriendly, so the pattern is fair.
Exceptions should be ignored, because they rarely change anybody's mind.

feedback.es: No condena observar patrones, sino convertirlos en ley: propone generalizar dejando espacio a las excepciones.

origin.audio: A researcher interviewed on a podcast recently described what she calls the airport effect. A traveller spends two hours in a foreign airport, meets three tired officials and decides that the whole country is unfriendly. The mistake, she says, is not in noticing a pattern, but in announcing it as a law. By and large, she added, people tend to be helpful when they are not exhausted. If you must generalise, leave room for the exceptions, because the exceptions are usually the people who change your mind. Her listeners laughed, but many wrote in afterwards to say that they had been guilty of the airport effect themselves.

prompt.es: ¿Qué objeta en realidad quien escribe la carta a la reseña?

choices.text: The mention that some residents are shy with strangers.
The use of absolute words where a hedge would be accurate.
The fact that the reviewer was a stranger to the town.
The claim that a few restaurants close early.

feedback.es: Admite que hay gente tímida y restaurantes que cierran pronto: lo que rechaza son never y every, donde most habría sido exacto.

origin.text: Your review of our town claims that the locals never smile and that every restaurant closes at nine. I have lived here for forty years. Many people are shy with strangers, and a few restaurants do close early, but the words never and every spoil an otherwise fair piece. A reviewer who wrote most would have been accurate, and I would not be writing this letter.

prompt.es: Completa: «Con pocas excepciones, los vecinos llegan a tiempo.»

feedback.es: With few exceptions es la colocación que matiza una generalización sin abandonarla.

origin.text: Nobody can say that every neighbour is punctual, but with few ___, the people on my street arrive on time and apologise when they are late.

prompt.es: Matiza la frase con una estructura de tendencia (tend to, by and large…).

answer.text: English people tend to be reserved with strangers
accepted: English people tend to be reserved with strangers
By and large, English people are reserved with strangers
As a rule, English people are reserved with strangers
The English tend to be reserved with strangers
English people tend to be cold with strangers
English people tend to be reserved and rarely talk to strangers
By and large, the English are cold with strangers
Most English people tend to be reserved with strangers

feedback.es: Sustituir all y nobody por tend to o by and large convierte un absoluto en una tendencia que se puede defender.

origin.text: All English people are cold and nobody talks to strangers.

prompt.es: ¿Con qué propósito menciona a su abuelo quien escribe?

choices.text: To prove that her grandfather was more impatient than her friends.
To argue that dinner should always be served at six.
To show that the trait is not limited to young people.
To admit that all young people are impatient after all.

feedback.es: El abuelo es un contraejemplo: si la impaciencia aparece en otra edad, no puede atribuirse a todos los jóvenes, y propone cambiar all por many.

origin.text: When people say that all young people are impatient, I think of my grandfather, who demanded his dinner at six sharp every evening. Being impatient is not a problem of one age; it is a human habit, and it tends to appear in every age group. I would gladly replace all with many, and then we could start an honest conversation.

prompt.es: Ordena: «Las tiendas de aquí suelen cerrar pronto los domingos.»

answer.text: Shops here tend to close early on Sundays

feedback.es: Shops here es plural, así que tend va sin -s y el verbo que sigue queda en base: close.

prompt.es: Escucha el mensaje: ¿qué le recomienda Leo a Mia?

choices.text: To replace her examples with the opinions of a few local people.
To keep the claim but add a few examples of rude behaviour.
To drop the topic because it may offend the people she met.
To qualify the claim so that it matches what she actually saw.

feedback.es: Leo no pide callar la observación, sino ajustarla a lo que Mia puede sostener: «most» y «reserved» en lugar de «all» y «rude».

origin.audio: Hi Mia, I read your draft. You wrote that all the locals are rude, and I think that is too strong. Why not say that most of the people you met were reserved? Then nobody can argue with you, and your article will sound more honest.
